questions: Separate the evidence about bias from the evidence about noise in this case. What does the mirror review tell you, and what does it not tell you about which physicians are right?
How much weight should Mr. D.’s case carry in the decision? Explain using availability, base rates and outcome bias.
Evaluate Feld’s claim that experienced clinicians catch patients a score would miss. What evidence would test it, and how would you collect it?
Okafor is an interested party. Which decision-hygiene steps should she take before making her recommendation?
Choose one of the three options and write the forecasts (with probabilities and resolve-by dates) that would tell the committee, a year from now, whether it was the right call.

perspectives.title: Adopt now: noise is the bigger, measurable harm
perspectives.text: The mirror review shows enormous variability in decisions about the same patients; whichever answer is right, many patients are getting a different decision depending on who is on shift. A structured pathway with documented departures reduces that noise immediately, frees observation capacity, and — crucially — creates the record that will finally test Feld’s claim. Mr. D.’s case is a vivid single event that the pathway would not have changed and should not drive the decision. Risk: the Northgate result may reflect a younger population and the new clinic, so monitoring must be tight.

perspectives.title: Extend the pilot with better measurement
perspectives.text: The pilot is uncontrolled, short, confounded by the new clinic and run on a younger population; rare events cannot be compared at this volume. Extending to the largest hospital, with a staggered start and structured recording of departures and their outcomes, would answer the questions that matter within a year. This respects the physicians’ council and Okafor’s own conflict of interest. Risk: a year of continued noise at three hospitals, and the possibility that “more data” becomes a way to avoid a decision.

perspectives.title: Decision support without the documentation requirement
perspectives.text: Offer the score to every physician as information, measure agreement and outcomes, and let practice converge voluntarily. This preserves clinical judgment for atypical patients and avoids a defensive-medicine dynamic in which overrides become indefensible. Risk: without recorded reasons for departures, the system learns little, and the physicians with the most extreme practice patterns are the least likely to change.

case.application: Player-development departments face the same structure. Evaluators looking at the same player reach very different grades (noise); one memorable miss — a released player who succeeded elsewhere, or a highly graded one who failed — dominates the conversation (availability and outcome bias); and the most experienced evaluator argues that a structured model would erode the judgment that catches unusual cases. The case’s moves transfer directly: run a mirror review on past evaluations, state the base rate, record departures from any model with reasons, and agree in advance what evidence would settle the argument.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion about the two evaluators is best supported?

stimulus.text: A fictional bank has two senior credit officers. Officer A has approved small-business loans for 15 years; the bank tracks every loan’s repayment and sends each officer a quarterly report showing defaults on the loans they approved. Officer B has spent 15 years approving loans for large, one-off infrastructure projects that take 8–12 years to show whether they will be repaid; the bank has never linked outcomes back to the approving officer. Both are highly confident in their instincts.

options.text: Both have equal claim to skilled intuition, since both have 15 years of experience.

Officer A’s intuition has a stronger claim to trust, because the environment provides many repetitions and clear, timely feedback; Officer B’s confidence carries little information without a track record.
Officer B’s intuition deserves more trust, because larger decisions develop deeper expertise.
Neither intuition deserves any weight; credit decisions should always be made by models.

questions.explanation: Kahneman and Klein’s conditions are a valid environment and an adequate opportunity to learn it through practice with feedback. Officer A has frequent, scored feedback; Officer B has few, slow, untracked outcomes, so experience mostly builds confidence.

optionFeedback.a: Years of experience are not the test; the feedback environment is.
optionFeedback.c: Stakes do not create learning opportunities; feedback does.
optionFeedback.d: Overcorrection: in a valid, high-feedback environment intuition can be skilled and worth combining with models.

questions.prompt: What is the main flaw in this argument?

stimulus.text: “Our training program teaches managers to switch from System 1 to System 2 when making decisions. Since biases come from System 1 and System 2 is the rational system, managers who complete the program will make unbiased decisions.”

options.text: It assumes deliberate (Type 2) thinking is normatively correct, but deliberation can rationalize a preferred conclusion and is not defined by being right.
It ignores that System 1 is located in a specific brain region.
It wrongly assumes managers can think slowly.
It confuses noise with bias.

questions.explanation: Evans and Stanovich treat accuracy as at most a correlate of Type 2 processing, not its definition, and motivated reasoning shows that deliberation can build sophisticated justifications for wrong conclusions. The two-system picture is itself debated.

optionFeedback.b: The argument’s problem is not anatomical; dual-process theories do not rest on that claim.
optionFeedback.c: Managers can think slowly; the issue is that slow thinking does not guarantee correct thinking.
optionFeedback.d: The argument is about bias; noise is not mentioned or relevant to its main error.

questions.prompt: A pre-employment integrity test is used on applicants. Suppose 5% of applicants would commit serious misconduct. The test flags 80% of those who would and 10% of those who would not. If an applicant is flagged, what is the probability (in %) that they would commit serious misconduct? Round to the nearest whole percent.
questions.working: Take 1,000 applicants: 50 would commit misconduct, of whom 40 are flagged. 950 would not, of whom 95 are flagged. Flagged total: 135. Probability: 40 / 135 ≈ 29.6%, about 30%.
questions.explanation: Most flagged applicants are false positives because the base rate is low. Counting cases in a fixed population (natural frequencies) makes the calculation straightforward.

questions.prompt: A due-diligence team has concluded that an acquisition target is strong. Which procedures specifically counter confirmation bias? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ask the team to list the evidence that would show the target is weak, and then look for it.
Ask the team to gather more evidence about the target’s strengths.
Assign a separate reviewer who has not seen the team’s memo to assess the raw data.
Give the team a larger bonus if the deal closes.
Test the conclusion against cases that could disconfirm it, such as comparable targets that failed.

questions.explanation: Confirmation bias narrows search to evidence that fits the hypothesis. Seeking disconfirming evidence, testing against cases that could falsify the conclusion and using an independent reviewer all widen the search. More confirming evidence and a stake in closing make the bias worse.

questions.prompt: What is the most defensible conclusion from this (fictional) summary?

stimulus.text: Fictional summary: “A multi-site replication project ran the same 12 judgment effects in 30 labs in nine countries, with a pre-registered analysis. Nine effects replicated in nearly every lab, with similar sizes across countries and between online and in-person samples. Three effects were close to zero everywhere. Variation between effects was far larger than variation between labs.”

options.text: Psychology’s findings are unreliable, so none of the twelve effects should inform management practice.
Whether an effect replicates depends mainly on the effect itself rather than on where it is tested; the nine robust effects are reasonable foundations, while the three should not be relied on.
The three null effects probably exist but were masked by differences between countries.
All twelve effects are now proven to work in organizations.

questions.explanation: The pattern mirrors the real Many Labs result: replicability varied by effect, not by setting. Robust laboratory effects are reasonable foundations; their size in organizations is a separate question, and null effects should not be rescued by appeals to hidden moderators the data do not show.

optionFeedback.a: Overcorrection: the study shows most effects were robust.
optionFeedback.c: The summary reports small variation between labs, which argues against masking by setting.
optionFeedback.d: Laboratory replication does not establish organizational effects or their size.

questions.prompt: A project manager forecasts five milestones: 90% (hit), 90% (missed), 80% (hit), 70% (missed), 60% (hit). What is the average Brier score? Give three decimal places.
questions.explanation: Square each gap between the stated probability and the outcome and average. Two confident misses dominate the score, which is worse than the 0.25 earned by always saying 50%.

questions.prompt: Your leadership team gives point estimates for every forecast and is almost always surprised by outcomes. You want to improve calibration within a year without a large program. What is the best next move?

options.text: Send the team to a workshop on cognitive biases.
Require every significant forecast to be stated as a probability or a range with a resolve-by date, recorded, and scored in a quarterly review against outcomes.
Hire an external forecasting firm to replace internal forecasts.
Ask everyone to be more humble in meetings.

questions.explanation: Calibration improves with explicit probabilities, records and feedback; scoring forecasts creates the feedback loop that the environment otherwise lacks. Brief probabilistic training helped in the forecasting tournament, but awareness alone rarely changes behavior.

optionFeedback.a: Awareness of biases does not reliably reduce them; without feedback, nothing tells the team how calibrated it is.
optionFeedback.c: Outsourcing may help some forecasts but does not build the team’s judgment or a record.
optionFeedback.d: Exhortation without measurement does not change calibration.

questions.prompt: A city must forecast how long a new light-rail line will take to build. Rank these approaches from most to least likely to produce a well-calibrated forecast.

options.text: The project engineers’ detailed schedule, presented as a single completion date.
The distribution of actual-versus-planned durations for comparable rail projects, adjusted modestly for verified features of this one, presented as a range.
The mayor’s public commitment date.
The engineers’ detailed schedule presented as a range they consider 80% likely.

questions.explanation: The outside view anchored on a reference class, then adjusted, is best. An inside-view range at least acknowledges uncertainty; a single inside-view date is overprecise; a political commitment adds motivated optimism.

questions.prompt: What is the most useful first step for the firm?

stimulus.text: A fictional consulting firm’s partners rate associates on a 1–5 scale each year. Associates complain that ratings depend on which partner they worked for. The managing partner believes the partners are excellent judges and that complaints reflect sour grapes.

options.text: Replace ratings with a fully automated productivity metric.
Run a noise audit: have several partners independently rate the same set of anonymized associate files, then measure the spread and each partner’s average relative to the group.
Tell associates that ratings are final and cannot be discussed.
Ask each partner whether they think they are fair.

questions.explanation: Whether ratings depend on the rater is an empirical question a noise audit answers without needing to know the right ratings. It separates level noise (harsh versus lenient partners) from pattern noise and gives the firm evidence before it changes anything.

optionFeedback.a: A metric may be gamed and embed its own biases; the firm does not yet know how large the noise is.
optionFeedback.d: Self-assessment of fairness is exactly what motivated reasoning and confidence make unreliable.

questions.prompt: Which description best captures intellectual humility as defined in recent research reviews?

options.text: A low opinion of one’s own abilities.
Deferring to the most senior expert in the room.
A metacognitive recognition that one’s beliefs and knowledge have limits and might be wrong, shown in proportional updating.
Avoiding firm decisions until all uncertainty is resolved.

questions.explanation: Porter and colleagues identify the common core as recognizing the limits of one’s beliefs and knowledge. It is about how you hold beliefs, not low self-regard, deference or indecision.

optionFeedback.a: Humility about beliefs is distinct from low self-esteem.
optionFeedback.b: Deference substitutes someone else’s certainty for your own; it is not recognition of limits.
optionFeedback.d: Humble decision-makers still commit; they hold the underlying estimate open to revision.

questions.prompt: Choose one recurring judgment in your professional life (for example rating people, approving budgets or evaluating players). In 150–250 words, (1) say whether it sits in a high- or low-validity environment and how much feedback you receive, (2) identify the bias or noise most likely to affect it, and (3) propose two specific decision-hygiene or calibration practices you could introduce, with one risk of each.
questions.modelAnswer: Example: annual budget requests from department heads. The environment is moderately valid — past spending predicts future needs — but feedback on my approvals is slow and confounded, since I rarely compare what a program delivered with what its budget assumed. The most likely problems are anchoring on last year’s figure and the request itself, and level noise between me and my co-approver, who is consistently more generous. Practice 1: each approver scores each request independently on separate dimensions (strategic fit, evidence of results, cost realism) before we meet, and we discuss only large disagreements. Risk: it adds time and may feel bureaucratic to department heads. Practice 2: every approved request includes two forecasts with probabilities and resolve-by dates (for example, “70% that the program reaches 500 participants by 30 June”), reviewed at the next cycle. Risk: department heads may forecast only safe outcomes, so the approvers must choose the forecasts that matter.

reserve.prompt: Which pair of conditions do Kahneman and Klein require before an intuitive judgment deserves trust?

options.text: Long experience and high confidence.
A high-validity environment and an adequate opportunity to learn it through practice with timely, clear feedback.
A clear explanation of the reasoning and agreement from peers.
High stakes and personal responsibility for the outcome.

reserve.explanation: The two conditions are environmental validity and the opportunity to learn it. Confidence is explicitly not a reliable indicator, and experience without feedback does not create skill.

optionFeedback.a: Confidence is not evidence of accuracy, and experience is insufficient without feedback.
optionFeedback.c: Skilled intuitions are often hard to explain, and peers can share the same errors.
optionFeedback.d: Stakes motivate effort but do not create learnable regularities or feedback.

reserve.prompt: A security screening system flags 99% of genuine threats and 2% of harmless items. One item in 10,000 is a genuine threat. Of flagged items, what percentage are genuine threats? Round to one decimal place.
reserve.working: Use 1,000,000 items: 100 threats, 99 flagged. 999,900 harmless, about 19,998 flagged. Share genuine: 99 / (99 + 19,998) ≈ 0.49%, about 0.5%.
reserve.explanation: With a very low base rate, almost all flags are false alarms even for a highly sensitive system. Natural frequencies make the denominator visible.

reserve.prompt: A forecaster’s 90% intervals contain the true value 55% of the time, with misses evenly above and below. Which description fits best?

options.text: Overestimation
Overplacement
Overprecision
Good calibration with bad luck

reserve.explanation: Intervals that capture the truth far less often than stated are too narrow: overprecision, the most persistent form of overconfidence in Moore and Healy’s taxonomy.

optionFeedback.a: Overestimation would show as a directional error, not symmetric misses.
optionFeedback.d: Over many intervals, 55% versus 90% is far beyond what luck explains.

reserve.prompt: Which practices are decision hygiene for a hiring panel? Select all that apply.

options.text: Each interviewer scores separate competencies independently before the debrief.
Interviewers read the referral note from the CEO before interviewing.
Scores are averaged and the spread is shown before discussion.
The hiring manager states a preferred candidate at the start of the debrief.
Interviews follow a common structure with the same questions for every candidate.

reserve.explanation: Independent, structured, aggregated judgments reduce noise and anchoring. Exposure to a powerful endorsement or a stated preference before judging correlates errors and anchors the panel.

assignment.title: Decision Journal Template

brief.text: This week you build the tool you will use for the rest of the semester: a personal decision journal for important professional decisions. A decision journal is a dated, contemporaneous record of what you decided, what you knew and assumed, what alternatives you considered, and what you predicted — written before the outcome is known, then reviewed after. It is the practical answer to three problems from this week: overconfidence (you cannot see your calibration without a record), outcome bias (you cannot judge process later without knowing what you knew then), and motivated reasoning (a record made in advance is harder to rewrite).

Your template should use the same fields as APERTURE’s Strategic Decision Journal, so that your entries can be kept there and your resolved forecasts can feed its Brier score and calibration table. Adapt the guidance and prompts under each field to your own work; that adaptation is the substance of the assignment.

items: Part 1 — the template: for each field below, write a one- or two-sentence instruction to yourself that makes the field hard to fill in carelessly (for example, under “What would change my mind”, require at least one observable signal and a date).

Part 2 — a first entry: use the template on one real, current decision that is **not confidential** — a personal professional choice, a public decision you are following, or a disguised version with every identifying detail removed. Include at least three forecasts with probabilities and resolve-by dates.
Part 3 — a short note (about 150 words) on how and when you will review entries: the review date rule, and how you will judge process separately from outcome.

brief.text: Privacy and confidentiality: never record confidential employer information, non-public player or personnel information, or anything you would not be comfortable seeing outside your organization. When in doubt, choose a different decision or disguise it completely.

Professional application: many recurring decisions in player development — promotion timing, assignment of development resources, changes to a player’s plan — are ideal for a decision journal because they resolve within months and can be scored. You may design field prompts with such decisions in mind, but your first entry must still meet the confidentiality rule above.

assignment.deliverable: A decision-journal template with field-by-field guidance, one completed non-confidential entry with at least three dated probability forecasts, and a short review plan.

template.heading: Decision and context
template.guidance: State the decision in one sentence as a choice, the date, and the essential context: what prompted it, the deadline, who else is involved, and what you know and do not know.

template.heading: Options considered
template.guidance: List at least three genuine options, including doing nothing or delaying. For each, note the main argument for and against.

template.heading: Choice and rationale
template.guidance: State the option chosen and why, in a few sentences. Note your confidence that it is the best option (as a probability) and the reference class or base rate you used, if any.

template.heading: Key assumptions
template.guidance: List the three to five assumptions that would most change the decision if they were wrong. Mark which are verified and which are guesses.

template.heading: What would change my mind
template.guidance: Name observable signals, with dates, that would lead you to reverse or revise the decision. Avoid signals that can only be interpreted in your favor.

template.heading: Forecasts
template.guidance: Write at least three resolvable forecasts: the outcome, your probability, and a resolve-by date. Make them specific enough that a stranger could score them.

template.heading: Review date and later fields
template.guidance: Set the review date. Leave space for what happened, how each forecast resolved, a process-versus-outcome assessment (sound or poor process; good or bad outcome) and lessons.

template.heading: Review plan
template.guidance: Explain how often you will review entries, how you will compute your calibration, and how you will avoid rewriting entries after the fact.

prompts: Think of a judgment you make with great confidence at work. Does it sit in an environment where you have had many repetitions with clear, timely feedback? If not, what has your confidence been built on?
Recall a time you changed your mind about something important. What evidence did it take, and was the size of your update proportional to it?
Which decision do you most want to judge by its outcome rather than its process? What would a contemporaneous record of it have shown?
After the Judgment Lab: where were you overconfident, and what one habit will you change in how you state ranges and probabilities?

review.front: How do Evans and Stanovich define Type 2 processing?
review.back: By its reliance on working memory and its support for hypothetical thinking (cognitive decoupling) — not by being slow, conscious or correct.

review.front: What is Melnikoff and Bargh’s main objection to dual-process theory?
review.back: The features said to define each type (intentional, controllable, efficient, conscious and their opposites) often do not travel together, so two bins misdescribe mental processes.

review.front: When can an intuition be trusted, according to Kahneman and Klein?
review.back: When the environment has high validity and the person has had an adequate opportunity to learn it through practice with timely, clear feedback.

review.front: Is subjective confidence evidence of accuracy?
review.back: Not reliably. Confidence comes from the coherence of a story and is felt as strongly in low-validity environments.

review.front: Name the three heuristics in Tversky and Kahneman (1974).
review.back: Representativeness, availability, and anchoring and adjustment.

review.front: How do natural frequencies help with base-rate problems?
review.back: Counting cases from one reference population (e.g., of 1,000 people) makes the denominator of positives visible, so Bayesian answers become much easier.

Confirmation bias: searching and interpreting evidence partial to an existing hypothesis, even without a stake. Motivated reasoning: a directional goal steers reasoning toward a preferred conclusion, constrained by the need for a justification.

review.front: What did Many Labs (Klein et al., 2014) find?
review.back: Of 13 effects in 36 samples, ten replicated consistently (including anchoring), one weakly, two priming effects not at all; variation was mostly between effects, not labs.
The degree to which a heuristic fits the structure of its environment; under small samples and high uncertainty, simple rules can beat complex models.
Overestimation (of your performance), overplacement (relative to others), overprecision (ranges too narrow). Overprecision is the most persistent.

review.front: How do you compute a Brier score, and what does 0.25 mean?
review.back: Average (p − outcome)² across forecasts. 0.25 is what always saying 50% earns; lower is better.
Calibration: your 70% happens about 70% of the time. Discrimination: higher probabilities for events that happen than for those that do not.

review.front: Order of steps in a disciplined forecast?
review.back: Resolvable question → outside view (base rate) → decompose → adjust modestly for verified differences → record probability and date → score.
Level: some judges are harsher overall. Pattern: judges react differently to particular cases. Occasion: the same judge varies over time.
Independent judgments then aggregation; structured, separately scored assessments; sequencing information; relative scales; the outside view.

review.front: What is the common core of intellectual humility?
review.back: A metacognitive recognition of the limits of one’s beliefs and knowledge — shown in proportional updating — not low self-regard or indecision.
